title: The world has knowing for its eye
hookLine: gods, elephants and sprouts, all held by one knowing
tomorrow: desire and will on a sacred list? what are they doing there?

lines: A BIRD. A WEED. A DOG.
ONE THING TRUE OF ALL OF THEM.
cards: Early morning, before the phone comes on. A bird on the fence. A weed pushing up through a crack in the driveway.

The neighbor's dog, stretching. The Aitareya Upanishad has its own version of that window, and it's crowded: sprouts and birds, horses, cows, elephants, wind and water and fire, the open sky, and the gods by name.
One thing, the text says, is true of every one of them.

teach.b: Having pointed at the knowing inside a person, the Aitareya turns outward. This is Brahman, it says. This is Indra, this is Prajapati, these are all the gods.
These are the great elements: earth, wind, space, water, light. The creatures born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, from sprouts. Horses, cows, people, elephants.
Whatever breathes, whatever moves, whatever flies, and whatever stands still. All of it is guided by prajnana, and rests in prajnana. Then a short phrase worth keeping: prajnanetro lokah.

teach.h: THE WORLD HAS KNOWING FOR ITS EYE.
teach.b: The world has knowing for its eye. Two things stand out.

teach.h: THE GODS ARE ON THE LIST.
teach.b: First, the gods are on the list. Indra and Prajapati aren't above the knowing, steering it. They're among the things it guides.

teach.h: HELD BY IT, NOT THINKING LIKE US.
teach.b: The elephant and the sprout are held by the same knowing the text found, a few lines earlier, inside a person. This is the Hindu teaching of Brahman in everything, said here as plainly as anywhere.
Many teachers connect it to things you'll see in Hindu homes: a tulsi plant watered each morning, a first roti set aside for a cow.
Notice what the Upanishad doesn't say. It doesn't say a weed thinks, or that a sparrow does philosophy. It says each one is guided by the knowing and rests in it.
So prajnanam brahma isn't only a private light behind one pair of eyes. In this passage it's also the eye the whole world is seen by.

how: Some readers of the Aitareya study this outward list together with the list of inner powers before it, so the saying prajnanam brahma is heard as covering both the inner life and the whole world.

o: four elements that make up every creature
four hymns that praise the gods of nature
four great sayings that name the self as Brahman

games.q: the Aitareya's window. tap the pairs.
p: on the list, guided by the knowing
held by the same knowing as a person
the world has knowing for its eye

s: the Aitareya says plants and birds think the way people do
it says they're guided by the knowing and rest in it, not that a weed does philosophy.
in this passage the gods stand above the knowing, steering it
Indra and Prajapati are on the list, among the things the knowing guides.
the passage runs from the gods all the way to sprouts
whatever breathes, moves, flies or stands still is guided by prajnana.

games.q: your little cousin asks: 'if the knowing is Brahman, is the dog in it too, or just people?' what does the Aitareya say?
o: the dog's on the text's list: every creature is guided by the knowing.
just people; the text keeps animals outside the saying.
the dog's in it because dogs think the way people do.
games.why: horses, cows, elephants, whatever breathes or stands still: all guided by prajnana and resting in it. the text doesn't say they think like us.

practice: Find one living thing you can see from where you are: a plant, a tree through the window, a bird, even your own hand. Look at it for the whole sit without naming it.
Let it simply be seen, and rest in the seeing, with the text's phrase in the background: the world has knowing for its eye.

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas, and prajnanam brahma at its widest: gods, elements, elephants and sprouts, all guided by the knowing.

orig.note: Sanskrit prajnanetro lokah: the world (loka) has knowing (prajnana) for its eye (netra). From the lines just before prajnanam brahma.

carryVoice: Carry this: every creature rests in Brahman. The whole world has knowing for its eye. That's day 1740.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 3.3 (this is Brahman, Indra, Prajapati, all the gods; the great elements; beings born of egg, womb, moisture, sprout; horses, cows, people, elephants; whatever breathes, moves, flies or is still; all guided by prajnana, established in prajnana; the world has prajnana as its eye; prajnana is its foundation; prajnanam brahma)
